days.note: The Round the Mountain Trail east from the South Climb trail, then the long, mostly off-trail traverse north round the eastern flank, across the Klickitat Glacier and Big Muddy Creek, to camp in Avalanche Valley below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers.
days.title: Cold Springs to Avalanche Valley
days.objective: Establish camp in Avalanche Valley (~6,600 ft)

days.note: An early alpine start from Avalanche Valley, up the Wilson Glacier to the headwall below Roosevelt Cliff (starts around 10,800 ft) — a steep, avalanche/icefall-fed line considered one of Adams' most serious routes. Top out and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs.
days.title: Climb the headwall, descend to the trailhead

schedule.label: Leave Avalanche Valley
schedule.detail: Early start for firm snow and to minimize icefall exposure below Roosevelt Cliffs.

days.objective: Summit via the Wilson Glacier Headwall and descend fully to the car

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip: a long approach round the east side to Avalanche Valley, then a serious, early alpine-start headwall climb (~13 hr) and a descent of the South Climb to the car.

sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Summit push and full hike out

itinerary.cal: Best July-September once the Ridge/Gravel Lake camps and Huckleberry Flats are snow-free; only a self-issue wilderness permit is needed.

days.note: From the PCT trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, hike north over Kendall Katwalk past Ridge Lake to the meadow camp most parties use to break up Huckleberry's unusually long approach before tackling the West Route.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach the Ridge/Gravel Lake meadow camp

days.note: Leave camp light and early, cross Huckleberry Flats and the PCT to the base of the West Route, then scramble class 3-4 terrain (with a class 4-5 summit block) to the top. Rappel into the notch on a 60m rope, reverse the gully/ridge, and continue the long hike out via Huckleberry Flats and the PCT — a very long second day.
days.title: Summit push and full hike out

schedule.label: Break camp
schedule.detail: Leave overnight gear cached, carry a light alpine kit

schedule.label: Cross Huckleberry Flats
schedule.detail: Reach the base of the West Route below the summit block

schedule.label: Reach the notch
schedule.detail: Class 4-5 scrambling below the final summit block

schedule.label: Rappel the summit block
schedule.detail: 60m rope to the notch, then reverse the gully/ridge

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Full descent via Huckleberry Flats and the PCT; many parties finish near dusk

days.objective: Climb the West Route to the summit block, rappel, and hike all the way back to the car

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip for most parties (~22 miles RT, ~6,300 ft gain) broken by a camp at Ridge or Gravel Lake; very fit scramblers occasionally push the whole thing car-to-car in one ~15-hour day.

hazards: loose, shattered andesite and rockfall danger in the summit gully — this west line has fallen out of favor versus the East Ridge for this reason
exposed class 3-4 terrain and a short technical step near the summit block
brushy, sometimes indistinct route-finding through tree bands on the lower approach
residual snow in the gully into July on some years

waypoints.name: PCT Trailhead, Snoqualmie Pass (Exit 52, Alpental Rd)
waypoints.directions: Leave I-90 at Exit 52 for Snoqualmie Pass and park in the large PCT North Trailhead lot off SR 906 / Alpental Road, at about 3,000 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park. Beyond that, the only permit you need is a self-issue wilderness permit. The trail leaves the lot northbound on the Pacific Crest Trail.

waypoints.name: Joe Lake
waypoints.note: PCT rounds Alaska Mountain's east ridge and drops to the west end of Joe Lake.

waypoints.name: West Face Talus Basin
waypoints.note: Flowery meadow northeast of Joe Lake; head up talus into the basin below the west face.

waypoints.name: Huckleberry Mountain
waypoints.note: West Face route, first climbed September 2001; stiff class 3-4 summit block.

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.rope_note: Stiff Class 3-4 route; trip reports explicitly recommend a 60m rope to rappel the summit block, which even experienced scramblers use.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: Backcountry permit required ($10/person + $6 reservation fee) through Recreation.gov and noca_wilderness@nps.gov. Wilderness Info Center operates mid-May to mid-October. Free parking at Rainy Pass trailhead. No park entrance fee. Northwest Forest Pass may be required at adjacent trailheads.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry/climbing permit required for any overnight stay; $10 per person camping fee plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee, booked via Recreation.gov and activated in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount before setting out.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter, typically early December to mid/late April, at gates near Ross Dam (MP134) and Silver Star (MP171); in 2026 spring damage and emergency repairs pushed the full reopening to June 14 — check WSDOT's SR-20 pass report before an early- or late-season trip.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No park entrance fee, but some SR-20 trailhead parking areas require a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass.

wa_storm_king_north_face.approach: East/Northeast from High Bridge via Park Creek drainage
wa_storm_king_north_face.overview: A rarely repeated technical line up Storm King's north face, first climbed in 1978 by Dick Emerson and Walt Grove. Unlike the walk-up-style Southwest Route, this is a genuine technical alpine rock climb, but little is known about its grade, pitch count, and exact line.
